analysis.one_liner: Repeals the Affordable Care Act and restores the health care laws it replaced.
analysis.headline: The full repeal bill drew only three sponsors and died in committee without a House vote when the 111th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would erase the Affordable Care Act as if it had never passed, undoing its coverage expansion, consumer protections, and new taxes, and restoring the law as it stood before 2010 [S2] [S3]. It was introduced by Rep. Todd Akin four months after President Obama signed the health law, picked up only two cosponsors, and was referred to eight House committees [S1] [S4] [S5]. No committee or subcommittee ever acted on it, and it expired when the Congress ended [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main winners would have been high-income households, who would keep the lower Medicare tax rates the health law raised on them, and health insurers, who would regain the ability to deny or rescind coverage and to charge sick people more. Drug and medical device makers would be freed from new fees the law imposed on them.
analysis.who_benefits_short: High earners, insurers, drug and device makers

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the Affordable Care Act effective as of its enactment and restores every provision of law the Act amended or repealed, as if the Act had never been passed [S2] [S3].
Because the Act raised Medicare payroll taxes on high earners and imposed fees on drug and medical device companies, repeal would have removed those levies [S2].

analysis.who_pays: People with pre-existing conditions would again be denied coverage or charged unaffordable rates; low-income adults in states that had planned Medicaid expansions would lose that route to coverage; young adults would lose the right to stay on a parent's plan; and the uninsured would lose the subsidies that made private plans affordable.

drawbacks.text: Restoring the pre-2010 law would take away the Act's core consumer protections — the ban on denying coverage for pre-existing conditions, dependent coverage for young adults, and subsidies for private plans — returning millions to the risk of being uninsured or uninsurable [S2] [S3].
Repeal would eliminate the new Medicare taxes on high-income households and investment income, a large tax cut whose benefit is concentrated at the top of the income scale [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits go almost entirely to concentrated interests — high earners who would avoid the Act's Medicare taxes and health industries freed from its fees and rules. Its costs fall on the people the Act was written to protect: those with pre-existing conditions, young adults, and low- and middle-income families relying on subsidized coverage. An honest supporter would acknowledge there is no replacement plan in the bill — it simply returns to the pre-2010 system.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in committee for eight months, never got a hearing or a vote, and expired when the 111th Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Rep. Todd Akin introduced the bill on May 5, 2010, roughly two months after the Affordable Care Act became law, with two Republican cosponsors [S1] [S4] [S5].
The Speaker referred it to eight committees, and it was later sent to the Health Subcommittee of Energy and Commerce and the Health Subcommittee of Education and Labor [S5].
No committee, subcommittee, or floor action ever followed; the last recorded action is the May 27, 2010 subcommittee referral [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the Affordable Care Act remained in force: people with pre-existing conditions and young adults kept their protections, and private insurers kept the guaranteed, subsidy-financed customer base the Act built around them.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Patients; insurers kept the ACA's subsidized customers

for.name: Rep. W. Todd Akin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the full-repeal bill on May 5, 2010

against.name: Speaker Nancy Pelosi
against.what_they_did: Controlled committee assignments and the House calendar; the bill was never scheduled for any committee or floor vote before the Congress ended

against.name: 253 of 435 House Democrats
against.what_they_did: Held the majority that had just passed the Affordable Care Act; no committee under their control reported the bill and no member brought it to the floor

sides.party_line_note: The repeal push was entirely Republican — the sponsor and both cosponsors were Republicans — while the Democratic majority that had passed the health law months earlier never allowed it a vote.

industries.note: Repeal would have freed insurers from the Act's new rules, but also stripped the individual mandate and subsidies that delivered them millions of guaranteed, government-financed customers, so gains and losses roughly cancel. Its interest in this bill ran against the public's, since the rules being repealed are the ones that stop insurers from denying coverage to sick people.

Repeal would have removed the Act's added Medicare taxes on high earners and on investment income, a tax cut concentrated at the top. Its benefit comes directly from a tax the public side of the ledger supports.

industries.industry: Brand-name drug makers and medical device makers
industries.note: Repeal would have eliminated the Act's fees on drug and device manufacturers, but also erased the coverage expansion that brought them tens of millions of new paying customers under the law's negotiated arrangement.

industries.industry: Uninsured and people with pre-existing conditions
industries.note: Repeal would have removed the subsidies, Medicaid expansion, and pre-existing condition protections that gave this group its main route to coverage.
